name: Proofreading Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building proofreading — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary proofreading tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building proofreading — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary proofreading tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When proofreading guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
2. Prefer the simplest proofreading approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
3. Document any non-obvious proofreading decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
4. Validate proofreading outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
5. When proofreading decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
6. Re-check edge cases relevant to proofreading (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
7. When multiple proofreading strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. Measure before optimizing any proofreading bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
9. Keep proofreading changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
10. State assumptions about proofreading explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
11. Keep proofreading outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated proofreading concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not silently drop proofreading edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of proofreading correctness.
- Avoid introducing new proofreading abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not apply generic proofreading advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for proofreading, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
